market_context: United States; FDA two-hour rule and one-hour rule above 90°F
title: How long can food stay out of the refrigerator?

seo.title: How long can food stay out of the refrigerator?
seo.meta_description: Perishable and cooked food should not sit at room temperature longer than 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F. Refrigerating or reheating later does not reset the risk.
seo.search_intent: Learn how long cooked and perishable foods can stay out, when they should be discarded, and why reheating does not always make them safe.

excerpt: As a general rule, cooked food and other perishables should not stay at room temperature for more than 2 hours. FDA shortens that limit to 1 hour when the air temperature is above 90°F (32°C). Once food has spent too long warm, refrigerating, freezing or reheating it later does not erase bacterial growth or toxins that may already have formed.
content_html:
A casserole stays on the table after dinner, potato salad sits through an afternoon party or a pot of stew spends hours cooling on the counter. The food may still look completely normal, but the clock is already running. Bacteria grow much faster at warm temperatures than they do under refrigeration.

The rule worth memorizing: 2 hours

FDA guidance says refrigerated perishables should not remain at room temperature for more than 2 hours. Once that window has been exceeded, food that was not continuously held cold or hot should be discarded.

You do not need to wait for a bad smell. Foodborne pathogens can multiply without creating an obvious change in odor, taste or appearance.

In hot weather, think 1 hour

When the air temperature is above 90°F (32°C), FDA cuts the room-temperature limit to one hour. A parked car, sunny picnic table or area beside a grill can become even hotter than the reported outdoor temperature.

A grocery bag on a car seat is not a cooler, even for a trip that feels short.

Which foods need this rule?

Meat, poultry, seafood, cooked eggs, refrigerated dairy, cooked rice and pasta, cooked beans, prepared meals, perishable sauces, deli salads, cut produce that requires refrigeration and leftovers all need time-and-temperature control.

The rule does not apply in the same way to shelf-stable foods such as dry bread, nuts, uncooked rice, unopened canned goods or whole produce normally stored at room temperature.

Food held genuinely cold or hot is a different situation

Cold food should stay at 40°F (4°C) or below. Hot food held for service should stay at 140°F (60°C) or above.

That is what makes a long buffet safe: food is not left lukewarm for hours; it is held continuously and verifiably cold or hot.

Putting food back in the refrigerator does not reset the clock

If lasagna sits on the table for four hours, chilling it afterward only slows growth from that point forward. It does not remove bacteria that already multiplied or toxins some organisms may have produced.

Freezing works the same way. Cold preserves the state of the food; it does not return poorly handled food to a fresh condition.

Reheating is not a universal rescue

Thorough reheating kills many active bacteria, but certain toxins can survive heat. “I'll boil it later” is therefore not a reliable safety plan for food that spent all afternoon warm.

The most effective protection happens earlier: control the time, hold food cold or hot and refrigerate promptly.

How to cool a large amount without leaving it out for hours

Divide stew, rice, pasta or cooked meat into shallow containers and smaller portions. They lose heat much faster than food left inside a deep stockpot.

You do not need to wait until food reaches room temperature before refrigerating it. The goal is to avoid several hours of slow cooling on the counter.

If you do not know how long it has been out, smell cannot reconstruct the timeline

There is no household test that can recover an unknown time-and-temperature history. Taking a small taste is not a safety test either.

For a perishable food that may have spent several hours without temperature control, discarding it is the prudent choice.

What to remember

2 hours normally; 1 hour above 90°F. If food needs to stay out longer, keep it continuously cold or hot.

Refrigeration, freezing and reheating preserve properly handled food; they do not erase several forgotten hours at room temperature.

faq.question: Can I eat food that sat out for 3 hours?
faq.answer: For perishable food, three hours exceeds FDA's general two-hour limit. Discard it if it was not continuously kept cold or hot.

faq.question: What if it is very hot outside?
faq.answer: The limit drops to one hour when the air temperature is above 90°F (32°C).

faq.question: Does reheating make food safe again?
faq.answer: Not always. Heat kills many bacteria, but some toxins can survive, and reheating does not erase unsafe storage history.
